title: Saying No: Negation
description: Two ways to say no in Egyptian — مش in front of a noun or adjective, ما…ش wrapped around a verb — plus never, nobody, nothing at all, and the polite refusals that let everyone keep face.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — contrast pairs. Every positive sentence from Lessons 1–2 is heard again with its negative; the learner sorts by ear before ever seeing the rule.
unlock_condition: ≥14/16 on the مش-or-ما…ش sort and one recorded polite refusal of food that a native would accept

grammar.title: مش for things, ما…ش for verbs
grammar.explanation: Egyptian has two negatives and the choice is simple. If what you are denying is a verb — a بـ present, a past, an 'I have' like عندي — you wrap it: ما in front and ش glued on the end: ما بشربش، ما شفتش، معنديش. If it is anything else — a noun, an adjective, a word like عايز or a participle like عارف — you put مش in front: مش مصري، مش كويس، مش عايز، مش عارف. The future is the odd one out: مش هروح, not ما…ش. People write the ما joined or separate (مبشربش / ما بشربش); both are right. Never ليس، لا، لم: those live in the newspaper.

examples.english: I don't drink coffee at night

culture.title: The first no is not a no
culture.note: When an Egyptian host offers food, the polite first answer is a refusal — لأ شكراً، أنا شبعان — and the polite response to that refusal is to insist. Only the second or third 'no' is real, so if you mean it, add a reason and a blessing: والله شبعان، تسلم إيديك. The same dance runs the other way: if someone declines your offer once, offer again. A real refusal of anything else is softened, never blunt: معلش، مش هقدر (sorry, I can't), مرة تانية إن شاء الله (another time, God willing). A flat لأ with nothing around it sounds angry.

phrases.english: No thanks, I'm full (the ritual first refusal)
Honestly I'm full — bless your hands (the real one)

phrases.arabic: معلش، مرة تانية إن شاء الله
phrases.transliteration: maʿlish, marra tanya in shaaʾ allaah

vocabulary.english: not (before nouns, adjectives, عايز, participles, the future)
vocabulary.teaching_note: The all-purpose 'not' for anything that is not a verb: مش كويس، مش هنا، مش عايز، مش فاهم. Also مش هـ for the future. Gulf speakers say مو or مب — never in Cairo. Never ليس.
vocabulary.image_scene: A red diagonal 'no' bar over a plate of food, a person shaking their head.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any vlog: مش before an adjective — مش كويس، مش عارف — with the face to match.

vocabulary.english: I don't drink (the ما…ش verb negation)
vocabulary.teaching_note: The model for negating every verb: ما in front, ش at the end, the verb unchanged in between. Take بشرب from Lesson 1 and wrap it. The extra i in ma-shuftish or the dropped vowel in ma-bashrabsh are just the mouth making room for the ش.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand held up flat over a coffee cup being offered, a polite shake of the head.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone declining with a ما…ش verb — ما بشربش، ما بحبش — the ش audible at the end.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'my life not…'. It takes the past verb without ش: عمري ما رحت أسوان. Change the suffix for other people: عمره ما، عمرها ما. For 'never (in future)' say مش هـ … أبداً.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person with a hand on the chest, shaking their head firmly, a calendar with all pages blank.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone declaring a never — عمري ما … — with a hand on the chest.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ما + حد (someone) + ش squeezed into one word. It goes first and the verb after it is positive: محدش جه (nobody came). Its positive twin حد is 'anyone': فيه حد؟ (is anyone there?).
vocabulary.image_scene: An empty room with a chair and an open door, nobody inside.
vocabulary.video_hint: A skit where a character finds the place empty — محدش هنا؟

vocabulary.teaching_note: حاجة is 'a thing'; ولا حاجة is 'not a thing'. With a verb, keep the ما…ش: ما أكلتش ولا حاجة. On its own it answers 'what happened?' or 'what do you want?'. The Gulf شي is never used in Cairo.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two empty hands turned palms-up, a shrug.

example.arabic: ما أكلتش ولا حاجة من الصبح
example.english: I haven't eaten anything since morning

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone shrugging — ولا حاجة — after being asked what is wrong or what they had.

vocabulary.teaching_note: One word doing two jobs: alone it answers 'not yet' (اتغديت؟ — لسه); before a verb or participle it means 'still' (لسه نايم). With ما…ش it is 'hasn't yet': لسه ما جاش. Doubled س.
vocabulary.image_scene: A pot on a stove with a timer still running, a hand raised in 'wait'.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone answering لسه to 'have you…?', or لسه نايم about a sleeping child.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The most useful small word in Egyptian. After a noun it is 'only': واحد بس. Between two ideas it is the everyday 'but': حلو بس غالي. Shouted alone it is 'enough!'. Doubled س — hold it.
vocabulary.image_scene: One single coin on an otherwise empty table, a finger held up for 'one'.

example.arabic: عايز شاي بس، من غير أكل
example.transliteration: ʿaayiz shaay bass, min gheer akl
example.english: I just want tea, no food

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone limiting an order or a request — واحد بس — with one finger raised.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Perfectly Egyptian, a little more emphatic than بس: the contrast really matters. Kept here so you recognise it; in casual speech بس does the job nine times out of ten.
vocabulary.image_scene: A see-saw with a small weight on one side and a large weight on the other.

example.arabic: كنت عايز أجي، لكن الجو حر أوي
example.transliteration: kunt ʿaayiz aagi, laakin eg-gaww ḥarr ʾawi
example.english: I wanted to come, but the weather is very hot

vocabulary.video_hint: A speaker setting up a contrast — … لكن … — with a change of tone.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The word for stopping a pour, a serving or an argument: كفاية كده (that's enough). Pair it with the pinched-fingers gesture. خلاص is the other 'done' word — خلاص ends a matter, كفاية stops a quantity.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand held flat over a glass being filled with tea, the pourer stopping.
vocabulary.video_hint: A host pouring tea and the guest saying كفاية كده with a raised hand.

vocabulary.teaching_note: One word, said with wide eyes: مستحيل! It answers a price, a story or a request. Long ii at the end. For 'no way' in the sense of 'never' use أبداً.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person with both palms up and eyebrows raised, a price tag with an absurd number.
vocabulary.video_hint: Bargaining or comedy: a shocked مستحيل! at a price or a claim.

vocabulary.teaching_note: عايز is not a verb, so it takes مش, not ما…ش. For a woman: مش عايزة. Soften it with شكراً and a reason, or it sounds like a child refusing dinner.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person gently pushing away a plate with a polite smile.
vocabulary.video_hint: A café or home scene with مش عايز and a hand over the cup.

vocabulary.teaching_note: مهم is 'important'; مش مهم waves something away. The warmer cousin is ولا يهمك ('don't let it bother you'), said when someone apologises. Doubled م at the end of مهم.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand brushing something off a table with a relaxed face.

example.english: You forgot the change? Doesn't matter

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone waving away an apology — مش مهم / ولا يهمك — with a hand gesture.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sits at the end of a negative sentence to make it total: ما فهمتش خالص (I didn't understand at all). In a positive sentence it means 'completely'. The خ and the ص both belong to the back of the mouth — a very Egyptian pair.
vocabulary.image_scene: An empty glass turned upside down, a single drop falling — nothing left at all.

example.english: I have no money at all

vocabulary.video_hint: A negative sentence closed with an emphatic خالص in any vlog or skit.

vocabulary.english: don't / forget it / free of charge
vocabulary.teaching_note: Three lives in one word. بلاش + verb is 'don't bother' (بلاش تروح); alone it is 'forget it'; and about a price it means 'free'. Long aa, ش at the end — it looks like a ما…ش word and behaves like one.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand waving 'leave it' over a bill on a café table.

example.english: Skip the sugar, I drink it plain

vocabulary.video_hint: A café or home scene with بلاش waving away an offer, or a seller saying ببلاش.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ينفع means 'it works / it's fine'; ما ينفعش is the polite Egyptian 'you can't do that'. It covers rules, timing and taste: ما ينفعش تروح دلوقتي. The positive ينفع؟ is how you ask permission.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand making a small side-to-side 'no' wave in front of a closed door.

example.arabic: ما ينفعش تاكل في الشارع في رمضان
example.english: You can't eat in the street in Ramadan

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone being told a rule — ما ينفعش — with a gentle wag of the finger.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Ends a negative sentence like خالص but points to time: مش هروح أبداً (I'll never go). On its own it answers 'not at all' to 'did I bother you?'. Written أبدا online.
vocabulary.image_scene: A calendar with a red line struck through every page to the end of the year.
vocabulary.video_hint: A firm أبداً closing a denial in a skit or interview.

dialogue.speaker: Aunt Nadia

dialogue.transliteration: shabʿaan eeh? inta ma-akaltish wala ḥaaga!
dialogue.english: Full, what full? You haven't eaten anything!

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.arabic: والله شبعان، بس شاي لو سمحتي
dialogue.transliteration: wallaahi shabʿaan, bass shaay law samaḥti
dialogue.english: Honestly I'm full — just tea, please

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.arabic: مش عايز سكر، مبشربش سكر خالص
dialogue.transliteration: mish ʿaayiz sukkar, ma-bashrabsh sukkar khaaliṣ
dialogue.english: I don't want sugar, I don't take sugar at all

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.arabic: معلش، مش مهم، كفاية كده. تسلم إيديك
dialogue.transliteration: maʿlish, mish muhimm, kifaaya kida. tislam ideeki
dialogue.english: Sorry — it doesn't matter, that's enough. Bless your hands

sound_spotlight.sound: The ش that closes a negative
sound_spotlight.explanation: The whole meaning hangs on a final sh. In fast speech the ما is barely there, so the ش at the end is what tells you the sentence is negative. Listen for it before anything else.
When the verb already ends in a consonant cluster, Egyptians slip a tiny i in before the ش so the mouth can manage: shuft + ish. It is not a new syllable to learn, just a bridge.
Short i, quick sh, no stress — مش leans onto the next word like a prefix: mish-ʿaayiz. If you stress it you sound like you are contradicting someone.

lesson_sequence.detail: A 45-second skit: a guest refuses food three times and finally accepts. No text; the learner just watches the refusal dance and the hand gestures.
Sixteen cards; each positive sentence from Lessons 1–2 plays, then its negative. The learner taps which word did the negating.
Listening sort: sixteen short clips dropped into two buckets. Feedback highlights the ش at the end or the مش in front.
Drag-and-drop: build the negative of eight sentences (بروح الشغل → ما بروحش الشغل; أنا جعان → أنا مش جعان).
The skit again with captions; the learner taps every negative they hear and counts the refusals before the guest accepts.
Three offers play (food, tea, a lift); the learner records a soft refusal for each with a reason and a blessing. Feedback on the softeners, not the grammar.
Words-learned counter rolls up. Nudge: the next time you are offered food, refuse once — then accept.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time someone offers you tea, say لأ شكراً once, then accept the second time with خلاص، شاي.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Rehearses the refusal ritual in the lowest-stakes real situation.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tell your tutor five things you never do, starting each with عمري ما or ما بـ…ش.
real_world_prompts.context: Tutor-ready task card; elicits both negatives in productive use.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Listen to any Egyptian comedy clip and count the ش-endings you hear in one minute.
real_world_prompts.context: Optional homework card. Trains the ear to catch the negative marker at the end of a word.

video_needs.scene: Someone declining, arguing or saying no way: a guest refusing food, a bargainer saying مستحيل, a parent saying ما ينفعش — the negative word audible and the gesture visible.
